title: Top minds in markets sound off on the rout in tech and AI stocks
excerpt: Carnage in markets on Friday dragged major indexes to grim milestones. Here's what some of the top strategists, investors, and commentators are saying.
content_html:
What top minds in markets are saying about the sell-off ripping through tech and AI

By Samuel O'Brient

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-20T19:30:24.333Z

It's ugly out there in markets this week, and it's only gotten uglier as Friday's session drags on.

Major indexes notched grim milestones in the session, with the S&P 500 and the Dow both entering a correction and the Nasdaq Composite going negative for the year. Not even a massively hyped IPO from Anthropic could breathe new life could breath new life into the AI trade, and the AI lab's stock led the market lower on Friday after its strong debut.

As market pros survey the damage, some are beginning to predict that the AI trade is at a major turning point, possibly on its last legs as a host of headwinds rewire the outlook.

Here's what some of the market's top investors, analysts, and commentators are saying about this week's carnage.

Ed Yardeni: Huang's affairs have "certainly" burst the bubble for Nvidia

Yardeni, a market veteran and the founder of Yardeni Research, maintains a cautiously bullish outlook, noting he views the sell-off as a necessary rest for the market.

"With the benefit of hindsight, it seems that the Jensen Huang mess has certainly burst Nvidia's bubble," he said. "As a result, the air has been coming out of the AI bubble. In our opinion, that reduces the odds that it will burst with adverse consequences for the economy, including a recession."

Earlier in the week, Yardeni had said that he expected AI trade can continue to do well, even if the its most current phase has ended.

Adam Turnquist: "Damage is mounting"

Turnquist, the chief cross-asset strategist at LPL Financial, highlighted a bearish signal from the S&P 500 on Friday, as the index broke below its 20-day moving average (DMA).

The technical strategist noted that while investor enthusiasm for the Anthropic IPO was robust, it didn't extend to the broader market, and the weak sentiment tanked stocks again on Friday.

"Technical damage is mounting, but a break below the 200-dma alone does not necessarily signal an imminent bear market," he added. "Stability in the AI trade and the S&P 500 holding key support near 7,000 will be important factors for a durable recovery."

Michael Kantrowitz: P/E ratios face a long list of risks

The chief investment officer at Piper Sandler, Kantrowitz is focused on valuations across the stock market.

"In the end, P/Es are driven by risk, and the list of risks creating uncertainty has lengthened all year (Oil, Fed, inflation, AI, Iran, Midterms, NVDA, etc.)," he wrote in an X post. "We will see P/Es stop falling when we see the list of uncertainties begin to shrink."

Michael Burry: "I tried to warn you all"

The investor made famous by "The Big Short" has been a vocal skeptic of the broader AI boom, specifically the aspects of all the circular financing that's resulted in a complex web of business relationships between some of the biggest names in the space. On Thursday, he reminded investors that he's been sounding the alarm on chip makers and neoclouds for some time already this year.

"Coreweave, Nebius, NVIDIA, semis, I tried to warn you all," he wrote on X. "I didn't say short. But I provided the information one would need to sell."

Burry later responded to a comment on his post, stating "If you think this is still all about an affair and some politics, you're not thinking hard enough."

David Morrison: "Too early to call an end" to the bull market

The senior market analyst at TradeNation highlighted the S&P 500's break below several key support levels, but according to Morrison, investors shouldn't rush to call the sell-off the end of the AI-fueled bull rally.

"It may be far too early to call an end to this near-relentless bull market," he stated. "Sentiment has certainly taken a bashing this week, and the market performance has been shaky since early October. But nearly everything looks oversold at the moment, so a rebound could come at any time."

"In the end, P/Es are driven by risk, and the list of risks creating uncertainty has lengthened all year (Oil, Fed, inflation, AI, Iran, Midterms, NVDA, etc.)," he wrote in an X post. "We will see P/Es stop falling when we see the list of uncertainties begin to shrink."

Michael Burry: "I tried to warn you all"

The investor made famous by "The Big Short" has been a vocal skeptic of the broader AI boom, specifically the aspects of all the circular financing that's resulted in a complex web of business relationships between some of the biggest names in the space. On Thursday, he reminded investors that he's been sounding the alarm on chip makers and neoclouds for some time already this year.

"Coreweave, Nebius, NVIDIA, semis, I tried to warn you all," he wrote on X. "I didn't say short. But I provided the information one would need to sell."

Burry later responded to a comment on his post, stating "If you think this is still all about an affair and some politics, you're not thinking hard enough."

David Morrison: "Too early to call an end" to the bull market

The senior market analyst at TradeNation highlighted the S&P 500's break below several key support levels, but according to Morrison, investors shouldn't rush to call the sell-off the end of the AI-fueled bull rally.

"It may be far too early to call an end to this near-relentless bull market," he stated. "Sentiment has certainly taken a bashing this week, and the market performance has been shaky since early October. But nearly everything looks oversold at the moment, so a rebound could come at any time."
